abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents a highly aggressive phenotype of breast carcinoma, distinguished by unique metastatic patterns and poor prognosis driven by its immune microenvironment. Recent advances integrating anticancer agents with personalized immunotherapies are emerging as promising avenues for TNBC management. Freshwater molluscs, though primarily consumed as nutraceuticals and less explored scientifically, hold promising therapeutic potential as immunomodulatory, natural anticancer agents. In the current investigation the anticancer potential of the extrapallial fluid of Filopaludina bengalensis (FBF) , a widespread mollusca in south-eastern India, was evaluated against TNBC, exploring its underlying molecular mechanism. Dose-dependent antiproliferative effect in fluid-treated MDA-MB-231 cells ranged from 89.28% at 3.125 µg/ml to 28.4% at 200 µg/ml ( p < 0.0001), with an IC 50 at 49 ± 1.6 µg/ml. Cytotoxicity driven by reactive oxygen species generation results in membrane damage, mitochondrial depolarization, and apoptosis (confirmed by DAPI, AO/EtBr). Annexin V/PI staining further endorsed late apoptosis and necrosis at 25 and 50 µg/ml and inhibited cell cycle progression at G2/M checkpoint, comparable to that of doxorubicin. Gene expression analysis revealed p53 activation, Bax upregulation, Bcl-2 suppression, caspase cascade initiation, and necroptosis with inflammatory mediator modulation, highlighting an immunogenic tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, high-resolution mass spectrometric analysis (HRMS) profiling of FBF predominantly revealed peptide fragments or related components, largely correlating with its profound anti-proliferative activity. Thus, F. bengalensis can be a potential breakthrough in oncotherapy by averting apoptotic resistance while eliciting complementary immunogenic necroptosis in human triple-negative breast carcinoma. Filopaludina bengalensis

21
. Cells at a concentration of 1 × 10
6
/well were seeded in 96-well plates, incubated for 24 h to allow adherence, and then treated with varying doses of FBF or doxorubicin (3.125–200 µg/ml, in PBS). Detection of apoptosis by flowcytometry
Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit was used to analyse the apoptosis in MDA-MB-231 cells following the manufacturer’s guidelines. MDA-MB-231 cells were seeded in 12-well plates, incubated overnight, and treated with FBF (25, 50 µg/ml) and doxorubicin (1 µg/ml) for 24 h. After PBS wash, treated cells were centrifuged to obtain pellet, which was resuspended in 100 µl of binding buffer and further incubated for 15 min in the dark with Annexin V–FITC (1 µl) and PI (10 µl) for staining. Finally, 10,000 live cells were screened and analysed using a flow cytometer (BD FACS ARIA III). Annexin V detected early apoptosis via phosphatidylserine exposure, while PI identified late apoptotic/necrotic cells by membrane integrity
27
. Using quadrant analysis, cell populations were discriminated as viable (Q3: Annexin V−;PI−), early apoptotic (Q4: Annexin V+;PI−), late apoptotic (Q2: Annexin V+;PI+), and necrotic (Q1: Annexin V−;PI+), enabling quantitative assessment of apoptosis in response to different treatments.

MDA-MB-231 cells at 0.5 × 10
6
/well were plated and incubated overnight for cell cycle analysis. Cells were incubated with FBF (25, 50 µg/ml) or doxorubicin (1 µg/ml) for 24 h, harvested by trypsinization, and rinsed in ice-cold PBS. Cell pellets were fixed in ethanol (70%) and preserved at − 20 °C for further use. After centrifugation (1000 rpm, 7 min, 4 °C), cells were reconstituted in 500 µl PBS containing RNase (20% w/v) and propidium iodide (2 µM), then after 30 min of dark incubation, cell cycle progression was monitored using a BD FACS ARIA III flow cytometer

,
29

RNA isolation and semi quantitative polymerase chain reaction
Semi-quantitative PCR analysis was employed to assess apoptotic (Caspase 3, 8, 9, Bax, Bcl-2, p53) and inflammatory (IL-1β, IL-1ra, TNF-α, IL-10, IL-6) gene expression in MDA-MB-231 cells, treated with FBF (25, 50 µg/ml) and doxorubicin (1 µg/ml) for 24 h. Total RNA was extracted using the HiPurA Miniprep Kit (HiMedia), quantified with a NanoDrop (Thermo Scientific), and kept at -80 °C until further use. Complementary DNA (cDNA) was prepared using reverse transcription (42 °C, 60 min; 70 °C, 5 min) and amplified using 2X PCR master mix (HiMedia) with specific primers. PCR amplification was carried out as follows: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 1 min; 40 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 65 °C for 45 s, 72 °C for 2 min; final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. Using GAPDH as the endogenous control and untreated cells as the reference, results are reported as mean fold change ± SEM from three independent experiments
30
.
High-resolution mass spectrometric analysis
High-resolution mass spectrometric analysis was performed using a Waters Xevo G2-XS QTof instrument equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source operating in positive ion mode. Chromatographic separation was achieved on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (130 Å, 1.7 μm, 2.1 × 50 mm). The source temperature was maintained at 120 °C with a capillary voltage of 1 kV, cone gas flow of 10 L h⁻¹, and desolvation gas flow of 800 L h⁻¹. Spectra were acquired across the m/z range 100–1600 with a collision energy ramp from 10 to 30 V. The injection volume was 1 µL. Data were collected and processed using MassLynx 4.2 software
31
.
Statistical analysis
GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA) was used for statistical analyses, and ImageJ (version 1.54f, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA) for image analysis. Results are expressed as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, with
p
< 0.05 considered significant.

Introduction
Cancer remains a major challenge to quality of life, driven by its escalating incidence across the world, substantial economic burden, and associated morbidity, all of which drastically reduce life expectancy. World Health Organization (WHO) predicted that, despite therapeutic advancements, the number of new cancer cases and associated fatalities may shoot up to nearly 70% by 2020
1
. After cardiovascular disorders, cancer represents the second foremost contributor to mortality. As per the estimates of GLOBOCAN, by 2020, new cases would account for around 1.3 million and 850,000 deaths from cancer
2
. In 2022, approximately 14.6 lakh new cancer cases were registered in India, with a global third ranking in terms of incidence (100.4 per 100,000). Males were more prone to lung cancer, though breast cancer predominated among females, identifying 13.5% new cases and about 10.6% cancer-related deaths
3
. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), attributed to the estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptor (Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) negative, is known for its hostile features, poor prognosis, which contributes to 15–20% of breast carcinoma cases. The prevalence of TNBC is higher among black and premenopausal women. It is typically high-grade with rapid progression and leads to considerable psychological and therapeutic challenges
4
. To optimize patient outcomes and minimize adverse effects, therapeutic resistance, and economic burden related to conventional methods, emerging cancer treatments emphasize tailored therapies that target specific molecular markers. Current research is also addressing the tumor microenvironment and employing peptides for selective drug delivery, ensuring safer and more effective anticancer therapies.
The chemical diversity of natural products offers a pivotal source of bioactive agents, approximately 25% of the natural anticancer medications approved between 1981 and 2019. Recent studies have highlighted that anticancer peptides from animal-based sources, including venoms, amphibians, marine animals, and terrestrial mammals, have demonstrated promising outcomes, even where conventional chemotherapy is ineffective
5
,
6
. Among marine sources, molluscs, especially gastropods like freshwater, marine, and terrestrial snails, represent the second most diverse animal phylum. Over 52,000 species have been identified, which significantly contribute to traditional medicine and serve as an affordable food source
7
. Notably, marine molluscan metabolites have already yielded Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drugs such as ziconotide (derived from cone shells, indicated for pain management) and the antibody–drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin (to treat Hodgkin’s disease and lymphoma)
8
, while other compounds, including dolastatins and kahalalide F, have potent anticancer properties against a variety of malignancies, including tumors of the breast, liver, colon, lung, and prostate
9
,
10
. Nevertheless, only ~ 1% of molluscan diversity has been screened for bioactive metabolites, highlighting substantial untapped potential
8
.
While most research has focused on marine molluscs, there is dearth of scientific validation in case of freshwater molluscs, despite their widespread use in traditional medicine and as a sustainable and cost-effective food source
11
,
12
. For example, the freshwater snail
Filopaludina bengalensis
(formerly
Bellamya bengalensis
), abundant in Indian aquatic habitats, is consumed as a protein-rich dietary supplement and has long been employed by indigenous communities to treat conditions such as liver diseases, anaemia, asthma, hypertension, dysentery, tuberculosis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis
13
. Previous studies have identified antimicrobial peptides, antioxidant oligopeptides, and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors from
F. bengalensis
, which demonstrated anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, and immunomodulatory properties
13
–
15
. Research indicated the immunomodulatory effect of the lipid fraction of
Bellamya bengalensis
that aids in preventing immune-mediated degenerative diseases
15
,
16
. Despite this wide spectrum of bioactivities, the anticancer potential of
F. bengalensis
, particularly in the context of aggressive malignancies, has not been systematically investigated.
Although apoptosis has historically been considered the principal mechanism of programmed cell death, many tumors evade apoptotic pathways, resulting in treatment failure. Necroptosis, a form of regulated necrosis characterized by robust immunogenicity, has evolved as an attractive alternative
17
,
18
. Activating the RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL signalling axis, often triggered by tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), necroptosis disrupts cellular integrity, releasing damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that stimulate antitumor immune responses. However, necroptosis can also promote tumorigenesis if dysregulated. Necroptosis-mediated inflammation and cell death, a double-edged sword in cancer biology, may promote tumorigenesis by fostering an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, it may boost immunosurveillance by eliciting potent immunogenic responses against cancer cells
19
,
20
. Thus, impairing cancer cell survival through modulating the apoptotic regulators (p53, Bax, Bcl-2, Caspases) along with promoting an immunogenic tumour microenvironment by selective regulation of inflammatory cytokines, is advantageous as a therapeutic strategy.
In this regard, excavating
F. bengalensis
as a novel source of bioactive peptides and metabolites with potential necroptosis-inducing activity is the need of the hour. Unlike marine molluscs, which have been extensively studied and commercialized for anticancer drug discovery, freshwater molluscs represent a largely unearthed reservoir. Attributed to its ethnomedicinal relevance, established bioactivities, and ecological availability,
F. bengalensis
provides a rational and sustainable model for bioprospecting. However, till date, limited studies have explored the potential of different extracts from this species in modulating cancer cell death pathways or offering therapeutic benefits against aggressive cancers like TNBC. The present study therefore aimed to investigate the anticancer potential of the extrapallial fluid of
F. bengalensis
against TNBC cell lines. Specifically, the present study aimed to evaluate its cytotoxic effects, characterize the underlying cell death pathways, and assess its potential to induce necroptosis. Thus, a systematic investigation of the extrapallial fluid of
F. bengalensis
as a source of novel bioactive compounds with potential necroptosis-inducing and immunomodulatory effects could bridge this gap, offering a new avenue for developing affordable, natural, and targeted cancer therapeutics.

Detection of apoptosis by flowcytometry
Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit was used to analyse the apoptosis in MDA-MB-231 cells following the manufacturer’s guidelines. MDA-MB-231 cells were seeded in 12-well plates, incubated overnight, and treated with FBF (25, 50 µg/ml) and doxorubicin (1 µg/ml) for 24 h. After PBS wash, treated cells were centrifuged to obtain pellet, which was resuspended in 100 µl of binding buffer and further incubated for 15 min in the dark with Annexin V–FITC (1 µl) and PI (10 µl) for staining. Finally, 10,000 live cells were screened and analysed using a flow cytometer (BD FACS ARIA III). Annexin V detected early apoptosis via phosphatidylserine exposure, while PI identified late apoptotic/necrotic cells by membrane integrity

RNA isolation and semi quantitative polymerase chain reaction
Semi-quantitative PCR analysis was employed to assess apoptotic (Caspase 3, 8, 9, Bax, Bcl-2, p53) and inflammatory (IL-1β, IL-1ra, TNF-α, IL-10, IL-6) gene expression in MDA-MB-231 cells, treated with FBF (25, 50 µg/ml) and doxorubicin (1 µg/ml) for 24 h. Anticancer agents exert their effects chiefly by promoting apoptosis and blocking cell cycle progression, thereby restraining tumor proliferation. Investigation of cell cycle phases was, therefore, performed to determine the specific checkpoints at which MDA-MB-231 cells were arrested following treatment and assessment of apoptosis via annexin V-FITC/PI–based flow cytometry, by quantifying the distribution of cell populations in different phases of cell death.

High-resolution mass spectrometric analysis
The molluscan fluid (FBF) was analysed by high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) in positive ion mode (TOF MS US+). Samples were directly infused, and full-scan spectra were acquired across the low to high m/z range and exact masses were determined with sub-ppm accuracy, neutral masses were calculated assuming protonated ions ([M + H]+).
Figure
6
represented the HRMS spectrum of the molluscan fluid, with multiple distinct peaks and the base peak observed at m/z 192.1242 (191.1169 Da neutral, [M + H]+), most consistent with a small metabolite, modified amino acid, or immonium-type fragment (like phenylalanine, leucine/isoleucine, tyrosine evident of the amino acid composition). A second prominent signal at m/z 124.0723 (123.0650 Da) similarly suggests an amino-acid derivative or fragment ion. Peptide-range features were significantly evident at m/z 338.3333 (337.3260 Da), and at m/z 521.3384 (520.3311 Da), consistent with small chain peptide or glycosylated metabolite. Higher-mass signals at m/z 701.5003 (700.4930 Da) and m/z 1019.6779 (1018.6706 Da) are compatible with medium-sized peptides or singly charged protein fragments, with possible contributions from multiply charged substances. Overall, FBF contains both abundant low-mass metabolites/fragments and peptide-derived components, however MS/MS acquisition is required further to confirm molecular identities and enable confident matching against metabolomic and proteomic database.

Discussion
Recent years have experienced considerable progress in the contribution of marine ecosystem in the development of promising anticancer drugs. Advances in omics technologies (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, glycomics) have propelled the study of gastropod mucins, revealing their potential across biotechnology and anticancer research
20
. Traditional use, nutritional value, and reported pharmacological activities of
Filopaludina bengalensis
has indicated the anticancer potential of this species. This study was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of the extrapallial fluid of
Filopaludina bengalensis
, against human triple-negative breast cancer cells, exploring the underlying mechanism. A dose-dependent reduction in cell viability was observed with an IC
50
of 49 ± 1.6 µg/ml, emphasizing the cytotoxicity profile of FBF against MDA-MB-231 cells (Fig.
1
). Previous reports similarly highlighted a concentration- and time-dependent decline in the proliferation of HepG2 and Huh-7 hepatocellular carcinoma cells by freshwater snail
Bellamya bengalensis f. annandalei
secretion extract, with IC
50
values of 12.88 µg/ml and 22.99 µg/ml, respectively
32
. Its anti-leukemic potential was also documented, with IC
50
values of 22.21 µg/ml, 10.3 µg/ml, and 12.79 µg/ml against U937, K562, and HL-60 cell lines, respectively
33
. Teerasak et al. reported the reduced viability of mammary gland adenocarcinoma cells (MCF7) mediated by two HPLC-separated fractions of terrestrial snail
Achatina fulica
mucus, containing a set of sixteen putative amphipathic and cationic peptides with anticancer activity
34
. Earlier investigations confirmed that treatment led to decreased viability of Caco-2 cells, following utilization of lyophilized mucus- and foot tissue-derived extracts of garden snail
Helix aspersa Müller
35
. The therapeutic action of most of the anticancer agents involves triggering apoptosis to suppress tumor progression. The apoptotic morphology could be illustrated by AO/EtBr staining which distinguishes cells based on membrane integrity and chromatin condensation. This is further complemented by DAPI staining that specifically binds to DNA, highlighting nuclear alterations, such as chromatin condensation and fragmentation
36
.  FBF-treated MDA-MB-231 cells at 25 µg/ml and 50 µg/ml doses revealed a dose-dependent apoptotic alterations, including chromatin condensation and membrane integrity loss, indicating apoptosis to be the primary mechanism of cell death (Fig.
3
C). DAPI staining revealed a reduction in cell number coupled with chromatin condensation and nuclear fragmentation, hallmark of apoptosis, which were further validated by AO/EB dual staining
37
,
38
.
Compelling evidence from recent research authorizes ROS as a crucial target as anticancer attributed to their proapoptotic effect at toxic levels. Characterized by elevated basal ROS, cancer cells are particularly vulnerable to ROS inducers that drive ROS beyond lethal thresholds without affecting normal cells. Excessive ROS generation has been correlated with elevated LDH release and induction of mitochondrial pathway-mediated apoptosis
39
,
40
. Treatment with FBF also confirmed a dose-dependent increase in LDH release and ROS generation (Fig.
2
A & B) that indicates the implication of mitochondrial dysfunction in FBF-induced apoptosis, establishing oxidative stress and membrane damage as fundamental mechanisms underlying its cytotoxic effect. Mitochondrial dysfunction is further substantiated by the reduced mitochondrial membrane potential documented in the FBF-treated cells (Fig.
2
C). Treatment with the test sample induced irreversible apoptosis, marked by loss of mitochondrial membrane potential indicated by green fluorescence, in contrast to red fluorescence in untreated control cells. The present study aligns with published literature that reports the role of pharmacological agent in inducing ROS production through mitochondrial perturbation and subsequent amplification of LDH-mediated oxidative stress. The two-phase ROS induction model could be proposed for the present study- elevating ROS generation and LDH release, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis.
Cancer cells maintain elevated basal ROS and are highly susceptible to further oxidative stress. Even a modest ROS increase can exceed the cellular tolerance threshold, precipitating death. Mechanistically, ROS perturb Cyclin/CDK regulation, with oxidative stress–induced disruption of the Cdc2/Cyclin B1 complex leading to G2/M arrest, thereby reinforcing ROS-mediated cytotoxicity
40
,
41

The present study proposes FBF as a promising therapeutic agent against MDA-MB-231 cells, exhibiting dose-dependent cytotoxicity. FBF mediated hallmark apoptotic alterations, including chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation, and membrane loss, validated by AO/EB and DAPI staining. Mechanistically, apoptosis was induced by ROS generation, LDH release, mitochondrial dysfunction, and activation of both intrinsic (p53, Bax, Caspase-9) and extrinsic (Caspase-8) pathways finally mediated through Caspase-3. Conclusion
Triple -negative breast cancer is intrinsically resistant to apoptosis, underscoring the need to exploit alternative programmed cell death pathways. Necroptosis offers therapeutic promise by bypassing apoptotic resistance while eliciting immunogenic cell death. The present study findings suggest that the test compound, found to be enriched with peptide-related metabolites induces dual cell death in TNBC by triggering mitochondrial stress–driven apoptosis (p53 activation, Bax upregulation, Bcl-2 suppression, and caspase cascade activation) in parallel with necroptosis. This is accompanied by selective cytokine modulation, including elevated TNF-α and reduced IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-10, which collectively foster an immunogenic tumor microenvironment. Therefore, the dual mechanism of freshwater mollusca-
Filopaludina bengalensis
fluid not only evades apoptotic resistance but also fosters durable antitumor immunity in TNBC, harnessing immunological strategies in oncotherapeutics.
